newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian firms seek seven pct depreciation in rupee.
newsitem.headline: Indian firms seek seven pct depreciation in rupee.

text.p: The Indian rupee's new gains against the dollar coupled with the devaluation of local currencies by neighbouring nations will aggravate a slowdown in India's exports, bankers and businessmen said on the weekend.

"We have formally asked the Finance Ministry to readjust the rupee down by at least seven percent (against the dollar)," Ramu Deora, chairman of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO), told Reuters on Saturday.
The FIEO is a quasi-official body that unites export lobbies representing the textile, jewellery, leather, chemicals, engineering, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and other industries.
Merchandise exports were $27.07 billion between April 1996 and January 1997, up 6.19 percent over the 10-month period from April 1995 to January 1996, India's commerce ministry says.
But this was sharply lower than the $31.83 billion, or 21.38 percent, rise they registered in the same period of the previous year (April-March 1995/96).
"Readjustment is imperative for a level playing field," Deora said, pointing to the recent devaluation of currencies by neighbouring countries, like Pakistan.
"We had one year of stable rupee," said Surendra Somani, managing director of pharmaceuticals firm Kopran.
Somani said the rupee-dollar rate had not been adjusted for Indian inflation or for the dollar's gains against major global currencies in recent months.
The rupee jumped to 35.75 against the dollar last week after being stuck close to 35.85 for most of the past six months.
The over-valued rupee was chiefly responsible for the export slowdown, said Jayesh Shah, group vice president (finance) at leading denim fabric export firm Arvind Mills.
"Exports now break even only because of incentives like special import licences," said R.K. Das, head of forex and treasury at Adani Exports, a leading overseas trading firm.
"We are now focusing more on imports," Das added.
"Textile exports are falling -- we are trying to survive," said N.K. Goyal, chairman of garment exporting firm Sarju Ltd.
He said Indian textile firms face tough competition from neighbours Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Vietnam, in addition to China, an old rival.
Bankers said Indian exporters' fears were justified.

"Over a period of time, it (the overvalued rupee) will hurt competitiveness," said Vishnu Deoskar, country treasurer of ABN AMRO Bank "The only mitigating factor is that banks are reducing interest on export credit," he said.
The chief dealer at a foreign bank in Bombay said there was near panic among Indian exporters at the rupee's continued rise.

Heavy capital inflows are feeding the supply of dollars, and Indian importers have virtually stopped covering forward positions because of the rupee's one-way movement against the dollar, dealers said.
But exporters were exaggerating the role of the exchange rate in India's export growth slow-down, some analysts felt.
"A few paise appreciation in the nominal rate in the short-term won't harm exporters," said N.S. Paramasivam, vice president (forex) at Essar Group, a leading private business.
Anil Singhvi, treasurer at India's largest cement exporter, Gujarat Ambuja Cements, agreed.
"It won't be correct to say Indian export growth is falling only because the rupee has risen in six months," Singhvi said.
The Indian government has attributed the slowdown in export growth to a global downtrend in commodity prices. Commodities constitute almost 80 percent of Indian exports.
